title: Mobile beauty scope and skin-treatment boundaries
audience: Mobile beauty therapists who offer facial, nail, waxing, tinting and similar treatments at a client's location
learningOutcomes: Explain why cosmetic injectables are outside the scope of this course and must not be offered under it
Decide whether a proposed service is inside the approved service list and inside the regulatory position for the location
Identify the chemical hazards that WorkSafe Victoria names for beauty products, and the step each one requires
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: Department of Health Victoria, Information for registered premises and environmental health officers (updated 22 May 2026); Macedon Ranges Shire Council, Public Health Regulations (no updated date shown); Queensland Health, Personal appearance services legislation (no date shown); ACT Government, Skin penetration procedures (no date shown); NT Government, Register a hairdressing, beauty therapy or body art business (no date shown); Gold Coast City Council, Personal appearance services (no date shown); WorkSafe Victoria, Managing hazardous substances and irritants in the hairdressing and beauty industry (reviewed 12 September 2025); WorkSafe Victoria, Safety data sheets (reviewed 30 July 2022); WorkSafe Victoria, Hazardous substances: safety basics (reviewed 30 July 2022).

instruction.heading: What is excluded from this course
instruction.body: Cosmetic injectables, including botulinum toxin and dermal fillers, are excluded from the mobile beauty course. This is a team decision recorded in the course plan. This lesson does not teach injectable treatments, does not describe how they are given, and no lesson in this course gives authority to offer them. Whether a business offering injectables needs a licence, is restricted, or is classed as a higher-risk service depends on the state and the council, and that is outside what this course covers. Gold Coast City Council places procedures that put foreign material beneath the skin in its higher-risk category, which needs a licence, and its page gives cosmetic injectables as an example (no date shown). Any future consideration of injectables is a separate scope decision with its own licence check.

instruction.heading: Skin penetration and where the lines fall
instruction.body: Beauty work sits under different rules in each state and territory. In Victoria, the Department of Health lists beauty therapy and cosmetic applications among services that must register under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008 (page updated 22 May 2026). The same page exempts mobile beauty therapists from registration, but the exemption stops short of the principal place of business, and exempts mobile cosmetic application services only where the service does not involve skin penetration or tattooing. Classification is also council-specific. Macedon Ranges Shire Council places facials or body treatments, manicures or pedicures, artificial nails, electrolysis and waxing in its high-risk group, which needs periodic renewal, and places eyelash and eyebrow tinting, spray tans and temporary make-up in its low-risk group (no updated date shown). Other councils may classify differently. In Queensland, beauty therapy does not need a licence, but higher-risk services do, including cosmetic tattooing, semi-permanent make-up, implanting substances under the skin, body piercing, with the exception of closed ear and nose piercing, and scarring (no date shown). In the ACT, mobile practitioners doing skin penetration work fall under the infection control licence. In the Northern Territory, a business that receives payment for beauty therapy must register; the register's beauty list runs from facial and body work through nail services to semi-permanent make-up and cosmetic tattooing (no date shown). Before you add any service to the menu, check which list it falls under in your state, and do not assume that a service is outside the rules because it looks minor.

instruction.heading: Chemical hazards that set the boundary
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria's page on hazards in hairdressing and beauty (reviewed 12/09/2025) names nail acrylics and dip powders, where airborne particles and vapours can arise; eyelash glue, which can include a cyanoacrylate that may sensitise the skin and irritate the eyes; and chemical peels, which may contain TCA, phenol or glycolic acid that can irritate skin and damage eyes. The business must hold a safety data sheet for each product. WorkSafe's safety data sheet page (reviewed 30/07/2022) requires an up-to-date SDS for every product, kept accessible. Its safety basics page (reviewed 30/07/2022) says employers need a register listing every hazardous substance on site. Whether a chemical peel is offered at all is a business scope decision. The approved list of services is held in {{business:services.service_description}}. Do not offer a mobile peel until the business has reviewed it with the regulator.

procedure: Check the proposed service against the approved service list, and refuse any item that is not on it
Confirm that the service is not an injectable, and do not offer injectables under this course
Check the state or territory position for the service: registration, licence or council classification, as recorded in the sources listed for this lesson
Identify whether the service involves skin penetration, and if so, confirm the licence position for the location
Check the safety data sheet for each product named in the service, and confirm the product is on the approved product list
Record the scope check, the source and the date, on the booking or the service menu

workedExamples.situation: A client books a mobile appointment and asks whether the therapist can also give her a dermal filler while she is in the room.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the therapist say, and what should be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Dermal fillers are an injectable and are excluded from this course. The therapist must not offer or perform the treatment, and should explain that it is outside the service the business provides. The request should be recorded as declined on scope grounds. The therapist may tell the client that injectable treatments are regulated in ways that vary by place, and that the client can ask the relevant health regulator or a registered health practitioner. The therapist should not suggest where the treatment could be obtained, or give medical advice on it.

workedExamples.situation: A Victorian mobile therapist plans to offer waxing and eyelash tinting at a client's home in a council area that classes waxing as high-risk.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the council's classification enough to start the service?
workedExamples.reasoning: The Macedon Ranges classification is council-specific and does not set the position for every council. Its page places waxing in the high-risk group, which needs periodic renewal, and places eyelash and eyebrow tinting in the low-risk group (no updated date shown). The therapist must check the local council's classification, and confirm whether the Victorian registration and exemption rules cover the service at the client's address. The therapist should record the council, the classification and the source.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved service list, held with the booking system or kit
Safety data sheet for each product in use, on hand at the visit
Gloves suitable for the products in use, including for eyelash glue and nail products
Eye protection where the product label or safety data sheet requires it
Record of the council and state position for the location

commonErrors.error: Adding an injectable to the menu because the client asks for it.
commonErrors.prevention: Injectables are excluded from this course. Decline on scope grounds and record the decision.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a council's high-risk or low-risk list applies in every council.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the local council's classification and record the source. Macedon Ranges is one council only.

commonErrors.error: Offering a chemical peel because the product is sold to salons.
commonErrors.prevention: A chemical peel is a scope decision. Hold it until the business has reviewed the mobile position.

commonErrors.error: Treating an eyelash glue as a low-hazard product.
commonErrors.prevention: WorkSafe Victoria lists eyelash glue as containing a cyanoacrylate that may sensitise skin and irritate eyes. Use gloves and the controls in the safety data sheet.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Injectable cosmetic treatments are excluded from the mobile beauty course. This lesson does not grant authority to offer or administer them in any state or territory.
In Victoria, beauty therapy is listed as a service that must register under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008 (page updated 22 May 2026).
In Queensland, higher-risk services need a licence.
In the ACT, mobile practitioners doing skin penetration work fall under the infection control licence.
WorkSafe Victoria names nail acrylics and dip powders, eyelash glue and chemical peels as hazards in beauty work. These hazards are confirmed.

qualityStandard: Every service on the menu is on the approved list, with a review date
No injectable treatment is offered, advertised or described as available under this course
The state or council position for each service is recorded with the source and date
Every product used has a safety data sheet on hand at the visit
documentationEvidence: Approved service list with review date
Scope check record for each new service, with the source and date
Declined-request record for any excluded service
Safety data sheets held for each product in the kit
summary: Injectables are excluded from this course and are not taught here
Beauty registration and licence rules differ by state, council and service
WorkSafe Victoria confirms the chemical hazards in nail, lash and peel products
Completing this lesson does not register you or authorise any service

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks a mobile therapist for a cosmetic injectable during a visit. Under this course, what is the correct action?
options: Offer it at a higher price, since the therapist is already on site
Offer it only where the client has a prescription from a doctor on file
Decline it on scope grounds, because injectables are excluded from this course

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the Macedon Ranges classification is accurate?
options: It is council-specific and does not set the position for every council
It applies in every council in Victoria, so no local check is needed
It states that waxing is low-risk in every council area across the state

knowledgeChecks.question: Which hazard does WorkSafe Victoria name for eyelash extension glue?
options: Carbon monoxide released from the curing of the glue on the lash line
A cyanoacrylate that may sensitise the skin and irritate the eyes
No hazard at all, because it is a cosmetic product sold in salons
